name: Glass screen
description: Glass instead of metal. A dielectric is an insulator: its charges cannot flow, but its molecules polarize, and bound charge gathers on its surfaces, negative facing the charge, positive on the far side. Inside the glass the field falls (to about 0.4 here), but a slab this thin is no screen: its far side's charge, nearer the beam, pushes along, and the beam is thrown off harder than without the glass. Place charges to bring it into the detector.

remarks.detail: The glass's molecules polarize: bound charge gathers on its surfaces, negative facing the charge, positive on the far side. Inside the glass the field falls (to about 0.4 here); beyond a slab this thin it grows, most under its ends, so unlike metal the glass is no screen. Even an endless slab would leave about three quarters of the field beyond it.
ε = 4 at every field and frequency, with no breakdown and no losses.
Real insulators near beams collect stray charge on their surfaces, which deflects the beam (why beam lines avoid exposed insulators); this glass never charges.
The particle pulls on them as hard as they push on it, but they stay put, as if infinitely heavy. Real instruments shape their fields with electrodes held at set voltages, not with point charges.

Everything is symmetric about the plane z = 0, so the particle never leaves it. A real beam also has a width across the plane, where the same fields act differently (focusing in the plane can defocus across it).
